claims.claim: Patient safety is the health-care discipline concerned with preventing harm that arises as a result of medical care rather than from the patient's underlying disease.

The Institute of Medicine report To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System (released November 1999; the printed report carries a 2000 date) estimated that between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans die each year from preventable medical errors in hospitals, and is widely regarded as the start of the modern patient safety movement.

The 44,000-98,000 figure was an estimate extrapolated from earlier chart-review studies and has been debated: some critics argue it was methodologically shaky or overstated, while later analyses argue the true toll may be higher. It should be presented as a contested estimate, not a settled count.

An error is any act of commission (doing something wrong) or omission (failing to do the right thing); an adverse event is harm resulting from medical care; a preventable adverse event is one caused by an error or failure to apply an accepted strategy; and a near miss is an event in which a patient was exposed to a hazard but escaped harm, often only by chance.

The Joint Commission defines a sentinel event as a patient safety event, not primarily related to the natural course of the patient's illness, that reaches a patient and results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm; sentinel events are expected to trigger a root cause analysis.

The term 'never event' was introduced in 2001 by Ken Kizer of the National Quality Forum; the NQF list of Serious Reportable Events now comprises 29 events grouped into 7 categories, and in 2007-2008 CMS stopped paying the extra cost of treating certain preventable never events / hospital-acquired conditions.

James Reason distinguished a person approach (focused on individuals' unsafe acts) from a system approach (which assumes humans are fallible and builds defenses), and separated active failures (unsafe acts at the sharp end, with short-lived effects) from latent conditions (dormant weaknesses built into a system by design and management decisions). His Swiss cheese model portrays defensive layers as slices with holes that shift, with an accident occurring when holes in successive layers momentarily line up.

A just culture holds individuals accountable for reckless behavior while treating most errors as symptoms of system problems; it distinguishes human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior, and bases its response on the type of behavior rather than the severity of the outcome. It is a middle path distinct from both a purely punitive culture and a blame-free 'no blame' culture, and is associated with David Marx (2001).

High reliability organizations operate in complex, high-hazard settings for long periods without catastrophic failures by sustaining collective mindfulness; the five HRO principles (Weick and Sutcliffe) are preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, and deference to expertise, with aviation, nuclear power, and aircraft carriers as classic examples.

Voluntary event-reporting systems, including near-miss reporting, help organizations detect system flaws, but they capture only a fraction of events; the Patient Safety and Quality Improvement Act of 2005 created Patient Safety Organizations and confidentiality/privilege protections to encourage freer reporting, and AHRQ developed Common Formats to standardize it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many people actually die each year from preventable medical error in the United States.
positions: To Err Is Human (IOM, 1999/2000) estimated 44,000-98,000 hospital deaths per year, extrapolating from the Harvard Medical Practice Study and a Utah-Colorado study.
Some critics argued the estimate rested on methodologically questionable extrapolation and may have overstated preventable deaths or diverted attention from other quality problems.
Later analyses argued the true number is higher, possibly in the hundreds of thousands, though those higher estimates are themselves disputed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the 44,000-98,000 range explicitly as the IOM's estimate, attributes it, and states plainly that the number has been debated and is not a settled count - it neither endorses the higher figures nor dismisses the concern.

sourceRecords.title: To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System
sourceRecords.notes: Founding IOM report of the U.S. patient safety movement. Read via the National Academies publication page (the NAP catalog URL 301-redirects to nationalacademies.org/publications/9728). Supports: the 44,000-98,000 annual preventable-death ESTIMATE (framed as an estimate and debated), the comparison to motor-vehicle/breast-cancer/AIDS deaths, and the systems thesis ('good people working in bad systems'). Copyrighted; REFERENCE_ONLY, no wording reproduced. Report released November 1999; printed volume dated 2000.

Supports the definitions of adverse event, preventable adverse event, error (commission/omission), and near miss; the systems approach; the Swiss cheese framing; that To Err Is Human is considered the start of the modern movement; and that the death estimates remain controversial/widely varying. U.S. government work, public domain; facts re-expressed, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Never Events (Patient Safety Network Primer)
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Patient Safety Network
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via WebFetch. Supports: origin of 'never event' (Ken Kizer, NQF, 2001), the NQF Serious Reportable Events list (29 events, 7 categories), the Joint Commission sentinel-event definition (death, severe harm, or permanent harm) and that never events are a subset of sentinel events, and the CMS 2007 non-payment policy for preventable never events. Public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Culture of Safety (Patient Safety Network Primer)
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Patient Safety Network
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via WebFetch. Supports the just-culture treatment: culture of safety as the values/beliefs/norms shared across an organization; just culture as a middle path between punitive and no-blame that maintains zero tolerance for reckless behavior; the three behavior categories (human error, at-risk behavior, reckless behavior) attributed to David Marx; and that the response depends on behavior type, not event severity. Public domain.

sourceRecords.title: High Reliability (Patient Safety Network Primer)
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Patient Safety Network
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via WebFetch. Supports the definition of high reliability organizations (operate in complex, high-hazard domains without catastrophic failure through persistent mindfulness) and the five Weick & Sutcliffe principles (preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, deference to expertise), with aircraft carriers as a classic example. Public domain.
